articles.headline: Australia Proposes Giving Users an Off Switch for the Thing Designed to Never Turn Off
articles.dek: A new bill would force social media firms to let Australians disable recommendation algorithms, though not by default, and not without objections from Washington and Instagram.
articles.catch_up: Australia introduced a Digital Duty of Care bill this week, whose centrepiece is an algorithm switch letting users see only accounts they follow. It follows a campaign called Fix Our Feeds and Australia's earlier social media minimum age law.
articles.why_it_matters: If it passes, Australians could opt out of the engagement machinery that decides what they see, and platforms could face fines of up to A$100m for breaching a broader safety duty. Other governments watching will learn whether an off switch works when the default stays on.
body: The Australian government this week introduced legislation in parliament that would require social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content, so that they see only posts from accounts they follow, the BBC reported. The bill also creates a legal duty of care for online services. It is, in essence, a proposal to make companies offer a feature that their business model has spent two decades arguing nobody wants.

The switch is part of the Digital Duty of Care bill, which covers social media, gaming sites, chatbots and more. Translation: a duty of care means a company must take reasonable steps to prevent harm, rather than apologise afterwards with a blog post. Services would have to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment. Children would be protected from harmful material such as content encouraging eating disorders, and adults from a narrower category of seriously harmful material. Breaches could attract fines of up to A$100m (£52m, $70m).

The human case for the bill is told by people who found the algorithm hard to leave. Varsha Yajman, now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, joined social media at 13 and says she was fed calorie challenges and weight-loss content. She says she still receives such content despite having every safety setting on and a long list of banned words. Flynn Martin, a Melbourne man, says manosphere figures flooded his feeds when he was 20 and struggling with his mental health. He was pulled out only after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay. Both say social media was not the sole cause of their problems, but was a key factor.

The policy began as a petition. Activist Chanel Contos launched Fix Our Feeds, which demanded that algorithms be off by default and that users opt in. More than 15,000 people signed, and two former prime ministers backed it. The government adopted a version in September but stopped short of making the switch off by default. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the aim was control for people, not government: if they want to doom scroll, that is up to them.

That compromise matters, because the history of such tools is that they are transient or come with trade-offs in functionality, according to the BBC. A switch that is available but buried, or that resets itself, is a switch in the way a fire exit behind a vending machine is an exit. Australia says it has drafted the law more tightly to prevent that, though the sources do not detail how.

The platforms have been quiet. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google all declined BBC requests for comment. Instagram boss Adam Mosseri did argue that non-algorithmic feeds would show users fewer posts from friends, and said he did not believe his app was addictive, distinguishing colloquial addiction, like binge-watching a show, from clinical addiction. The BBC notes that a US jury recently ruled otherwise.

Opposition comes from the other direction too. Right-wing parties in Australia and the Trump administration say the reforms risk over-moderation and censorship. Defenders reply that users can still follow and post whatever they like, including manosphere podcasts and claims the moon landing was fake. Critics also worry the government has bitten off more than it can chew. Communications Minister Anika Wells says the bill shifts responsibility from victims to the companies that profit from Australian users.
Watch next for whether parliament keeps the switch intact, and whether the off position is as easy to find as the scroll button.
articles.wire_headline: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch

articles.headline: U.S. Posts $1.992 Trillion Deficit, Its 25th Straight, Citing Growth Plan Not Yet Observed
articles.dek: The fiscal 2026 gap grew 12% as interest costs passed $1 trillion, while 10-year yields sit at 5.1% and the political fix remains scheduled for later.
articles.catch_up: The Treasury reported Friday that the government ran a $1.992 trillion deficit in fiscal 2026, up from $1.775 trillion a year earlier. Long-term yields have climbed to levels not seen since 2002, driven partly by the war with Iran, heavy bond issuance and rising oil prices.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher Treasury yields feed directly into mortgage rates, which CNBC says hover around 7.5%, and into the cost of every other loan priced off them. The more the government pays in interest, the less room it has for anything else, including cutting the deficit.
body: The United States ended fiscal 2026 with a budget deficit of $1.992 trillion, the Treasury Department reported Friday. That is about 12% above last year's $1.775 trillion and the third-largest on record, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the government was fighting a pandemic. This time the cause is less dramatic: it is simply what the government costs, minus what it collects. It was also the 25th consecutive year of deficits, the last surplus having arrived in 2001.

CNBC reported that both receipts and outlays hit records, which is the fiscal equivalent of a household announcing its best-ever income and its worst-ever month at the same time. Social Security cost nearly $1.7 trillion and Medicare almost $1.1 trillion. Net interest, meaning what Treasury pays on its debt minus what it receives, topped $1 trillion, up from $970 billion. Translation: the country now spends more than a trillion dollars a year for the privilege of having already spent money.

Revenue did its part, within limits. Individual income taxes brought in more than $2.8 trillion, up about 7%. Corporate income tax fell roughly $70 billion to $381 billion, which CNBC attributed to the tax cuts in last year's One Big Beautiful Bill. Tariffs set a record for gross customs duties, but after the Supreme Court ruled many of them unconstitutional, refunds sent billions back to retailers. A tax that is collected and then returned is, strictly speaking, a loan from importers.

The deficit is about 6.2% of GDP, according to CNBC's analysis. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued the target should be below 4% by the end of Trump's term, and CNBC concluded there is almost no way to reach it. Bessent's preferred route is growth: 'we have to grow our way out of it,' he said in Dallas last month. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates that this would require a decade of 7.2% growth. The second quarter was recently revised up to 2.2%, which is a start in the sense that a journey of a thousand miles begins with a step.

Bond traders are less patient. The 10-year yield stands at 5.1%, up 114 basis points since the end of February. Translation: a basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point, so lenders now demand more than a full point of extra annual payment than they did before the Iran war began on Feb. 28. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and traders worry that central banks may have to raise rates. Brent crude was most recently at $126.55 a barrel, which suggests they are not being paranoid.

Supply is part of the problem. Investors want extra compensation for holding long bonds because the government keeps issuing them, while companies are issuing hundreds of billions in debt to build artificial intelligence infrastructure. The Treasury is competing for savers' money with data centers. The CBO estimates that if rates run a half-point above its forecast, the 10-year deficit total rises by $1.9 trillion; a 1.5-point overshoot adds $6 trillion. The CBO expects the 10-year yield to average 4.3%, against 5.1% today.

The mortgage market is the visible casualty. Redfin said pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in three years, with the average 30-year fixed rate near 7.5%. Mortgage rates track the 10-year yield, so Washington's borrowing habits are now a line item in the cost of buying a house in any state.

Meanwhile, Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC that hedge funds have become a bigger part of government bond markets, making a broad shock more likely than before. The IMF puts hedge fund gross assets at about $13 trillion, and the Office of Financial Research says they held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025. Many use basis trades, which means buying Treasurys, shorting the matching futures and borrowing heavily to magnify a tiny price gap. It works until it doesn't, which is the standard disclosure for leverage.

The politics offer little relief. Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House in the Nov. 3 midterms, and CNBC noted that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts. Trump, for his part, pledged $5,000 checks to every adult citizen if Republicans swept the election. CNBC notes that higher yields are also drawing buyers to Treasurys, so expensive borrowing is not yet a crisis. For now it is merely a very large invoice, with the deadline unspecified.
articles.wire_headline: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year

articles.headline: Markets Confident Fed Will Hold Rates, Based on Chairman Who Declines to Say
articles.dek: Futures price just a 15% chance of an October hike, though Kevin Warsh has rejected the habit of telling investors his plans in advance.
articles.catch_up: Kevin Warsh, the new Fed chairman, helped push the FOMC to a unanimous rate increase in September. The committee meets again on Oct. 28, and traders expect a pause.
articles.why_it_matters: If the Fed hikes against expectations, mortgage, credit card and business borrowing costs could move quickly and stock and bond prices could swing. With CPI at 3.7%, the case for tighter policy is not imaginary.
body: According to CNBC, traders are betting heavily that the Federal Reserve will leave interest rates alone when it meets on Oct. 28. Futures markets put the chance of a hike at 15% as of Friday morning. That is a confident bet, placed on a chairman who has declined to confirm it.

The reasoning goes like this. Fed Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams recently gave remarks suggesting little urgency to raise rates, and markets repriced toward a hold. Together with Kevin Warsh, they form an informal leadership group known as the troika. Translation: the three people who usually decide things before everyone else votes on them.

The trouble, CNBC's analysis argues, is that the old rule that the lieutenants speak for the chairman may not survive the leadership change. Warsh has repeatedly rejected the convention of telling markets what he plans before the committee meets. He also said at the September press conference of the Fed's own projections, "Those aren't my forecasts." Investors have been reading signals from a communication system its new operator has openly declined to use.

Then there is the inflation data. Consumer prices rose 3.7% for the year through September, and producer prices gained 6.3%. CNBC says that implies core PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, of about 3.1% year over year. Translation: prices are rising at a pace that is roughly half again the Fed's 2% target, which Warsh called "a firm, fixed target" at Jackson Hole.

Against that, Warsh said in Bangkok that "the world has broadly conformed to our expectations" since September, and he stressed that he was not signaling a decision either way. That can be read as comfort with a pause. It can also be read as a sentence that commits him to nothing, which is the point of the exercise.

Other numbers cut in different directions. The fed funds rate stands at 3.88%, the 2-year Treasury yields 4.77% and the 10-year yields 5.1%, so the bond market is already pricing in more tightening than the Fed has delivered. The Chicago Fed's financial conditions index has risen about 0.05 points since Jackson Hole but remains negative, meaning conditions are tighter yet still loose overall. Warsh has leaned on that looseness to justify his hawkish stance.

A hike that markets do not expect would produce volatility, and it would embarrass Jefferson and Williams, whose remarks helped shape those expectations. CNBC notes Warsh may instead wait to gauge the committee and settle near its middle. The VIX, a measure of expected stock market swings, sat at 16.46 on Oct. 15, which is not the level of an investor class bracing for impact.
The practical advice is to read the Oct. 28 press conference carefully. Until then, a 15% chance is merely what markets assign to a thing they have decided not to think about.
articles.wire_headline: Analysis: Everyone expects the Fed to hold rates in October. Kevin Warsh could surprise us all

articles.headline: AI Stocks Slide as Inflation Reminds Markets That Money Costs Money
articles.dek: The Nasdaq fell 4.5% last week, its worst since June, while the Dow rose 0.7% as investors fled to toothpaste-adjacent sectors.
articles.catch_up: Technology shares have been propelled for months by enormous spending on artificial intelligence. Last week, hotter inflation data and fresh competition worries hit that trade, just as earnings season began.
articles.why_it_matters: If borrowing stays expensive, the companies building AI infrastructure with debt face higher costs, and index funds heavy in tech could keep swinging. Ordinary savers with retirement accounts own a lot of this, whether they remember choosing it or not.
body: Stocks had a rough week, and the cause was largely tech. According to CNBC, the Nasdaq dropped 4.5%, ending a four-week winning streak and marking its worst week since June. The S&P 500 fell 2%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.7% as investors moved into healthcare, consumer staples and other sectors that do not need a data center to justify their existence.

The trigger was inflation. September's consumer price index rose 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% economists expected. Translation: prices are rising a bit faster than forecasters said, which is the one thing forecasters are paid to avoid. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, also came in slightly hot.

Producer prices were no comfort. CNBC reported the producer price index, a measure of what businesses pay for goods and services, jumped 1.3% for the month and 6.3% for the year, the largest gains since 2022. Higher inflation, partly driven by elevated oil prices, suggests the Federal Reserve may keep interest rates high for longer. The latest data put Brent crude at $126.55, the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.1% and the Fed funds rate at 3.88%, so the cost of money is no longer a rounding error.

That matters because the AI buildout runs substantially on borrowed money. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned Monday that access to capital could become the industry's next major constraint, according to CNBC. Translation: the chips are available, but the loans are the scarce part. CoreWeave, a so-called neocloud that rents out computing power, has seen total debt rise above $51 billion, and its shares fell 25% last week. Its bond yields and credit default swaps, a kind of insurance on debt, also rose, which is how lenders say they would like to discuss this further.

Competition added to the mood. Memory chip stocks including Micron, Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate fell after Chinese rival CXMT announced progress on a more efficient chip structure, raising fears of a supply glut. The iShares Semiconductor ETF lost ground for nine straight sessions, its longest streak in more than a decade. Cybersecurity stocks also suffered, with Palo Alto Networks down more than 18% and CrowdStrike down more than 17% after reports that OpenAI is in early talks to buy Trail of Bits.

Not every large technology name suffered equally. Meta rallied after releasing new AI models, though it still finished the week down more than 1%. Microsoft closed at a record high Tuesday for the first time in nearly a year, after previously falling by more than a third. Both ended the week down more than 1%, which on this particular week qualified as a victory lap.

Banks offered the earnings-season counterpoint. Goldman Sachs reported equities trading revenue up 72% and investment banking fees up 21%, yet shares gave up an early rally. Wells Fargo beat earnings estimates but missed on revenue, and Bank of New York beat on both and raised its outlook. CNBC's Jim Cramer said investors seem more worried about the economy ahead than the quarter just reported, which is a polite way of saying the results were good and nobody cared.

MarketWatch noted that the idea that AI stocks have been immune to rising bond yields is not quite right, according to one strategist. Investors now have a week of earnings to test whether profits can outrun interest rates. If they cannot, diversification, a strategy that everyone admires most when it is working, will receive its annual standing ovation.
articles.wire_headline: Stocks are heading for a high-stakes showdown, as strong earnings collide with rising borrowing costs

articles.headline: Berkshire Rallies as Investors Rediscover Boring Things, Including Cash, Soda and Oil
articles.dek: Berkshire Hathaway's A shares closed at $798,000, 1.4% below their record, as a sell-off in tech left the conglomerate's unglamorous holdings looking brilliant.
articles.catch_up: Warren Buffett told shareholders in May 2025 that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year, and Berkshire shares then fell more than 14% in three months on fears that a 'Buffett premium' was dissolving. Greg Abel now runs the company.
articles.why_it_matters: Berkshire is a bellwether for whether investors still want patient, cash-rich 'old economy' companies when tech wobbles. Its roughly $360 billion cash pile also earns more when short-term rates are high, which is good for Berkshire and less cheerful for anyone with a mortgage.
body: Berkshire Hathaway shares closed Friday at their highest level since Warren Buffett announced at the May 2025 annual meeting that he would step down as CEO. According to CNBC, the A shares ended at $798,000 and the B shares at $532.02, each about 1.4% below their all-time closing highs of $809,350 and $539.80. The market fell on Friday, and Berkshire rose more than 1%, which is the sort of thing a company can do when its main product is not enthusiasm.

The recovery has taken more than a year. After the succession announcement, the stock lost over 14% in three months as investors fretted that a 'Buffett premium' was disappearing. Translation: people had been paying extra for the man, and were now checking whether the company came with a receipt. B shares have cut their 17.5-point deficit against the S&P 500 since June 1 by almost two-thirds, and now trail by 6.0 points for the year.

CNBC points to several causes, most of them pleasantly dull. Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields says higher short-term interest rates are helping, since Berkshire holds roughly $360 billion in cash and 'they'll be making more money' on it. Translation: the world's most famous pile of unspent money is finally being paid to sit there. The Fed funds rate is 3.88% and the two-year Treasury yields 4.77%, so waiting is a strategy again.

Insurance operations have enjoyed a quiet hurricane season. Chevron, a $19 billion holding, closed at a record after gaining almost 36% since early July, helped by higher oil prices, with Brent at $126.55. Coca-Cola, now a $37.6 billion position, also hit a record and is up 34% this year, perhaps helped by KFC's switch from Pepsi to Coke. Rarely has a conglomerate profited so thoroughly from weather that did not happen, expensive fuel and chicken restaurants changing soft drinks.

The less boring part is Bending Spoons, an Italian company that buys discarded internet brands such as AOL, Evernote and Vimeo, uses AI to cut costs, and spends the savings on more acquisitions. Berkshire disclosed a further $330 million purchase of 10 million new shares at $33, a discount of almost 12% to the prior close of $37.86. The announcement also revealed, apparently for the first time, a $600 million purchase at the July IPO. The shares closed Wednesday up 41% at $53.46 and ended Friday at $47.07.

CNBC's estimate, which Bending Spoons would not confirm, assumes Berkshire paid the $29 IPO price. That implies about 20.7 million shares then, around 30.7 million now, a stake of roughly 4.5%, and a paper gain of 55.3% on $930 million invested. The next portfolio disclosure, due next month, may settle the arithmetic. Who at Berkshire made the call remains unknown.

Analysts split on what it means. Morningstar's Greggory Warren sees a firm 'finally moving out of its comfort zone' to deploy capital. Barron's Andrew Bary notes that many holders want more stock buying given the cash pile, but that Bending Spoons was a surprise given its high valuation. Berkshire has now bought a stock at a large multiple of earnings, which for this company is the equivalent of showing up in a loud shirt.

The pattern is a familiar one. When investors tire of high-flying AI and tech names, they rediscover companies that sell soda, insure houses and pump oil. Berkshire's challenge is that its next big move now belongs to Abel, and the market will keep checking which parts of the stock were Buffett and which were just a very large pile of cash.
articles.wire_headline: Berkshire shares buck market sell-off, rally to highest since Buffett said he would step down as CEO

articles.headline: South Korea Finance Minister Says Chip Boom Will Last Through Next Year, Citing Shortage of Chips
articles.dek: Lee Hyoung-Il tells CNBC the supply-demand gap is wide, even as a local newspaper column warns of a 'red ocean' by 2029.
articles.catch_up: Semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week on worries about interest rate hikes and growing competition from Chinese firms, dragging down SK Hynix, Seoul Semiconductor and Nvidia. South Korea's market is unusually dependent on chipmakers.
articles.why_it_matters: When one industry makes up a large share of a national economy, its mood swings become the country's mood swings, and the tax receipts that fund public services follow. Investors holding chip stocks, directly or through index funds, are exposed to the same dependency.
body: South Korea's finance minister, Lee Hyoung-Il, said on Saturday that the semiconductor boom should last at least through 2027. He told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok that the gap between chip demand and supply is still very wide. The remark arrived after a week in which chip stocks fell sharply, which is the kind of timing that makes a reassurance sound like a reassurance.

Lee's reasoning is straightforward: demand exceeds supply, and supply is still being expanded. Translation: there are not enough chips, and factories are being built to make more, which is both the reason the boom continues and, in other circumstances, the usual way booms end. Lee did not dwell on the second half of that sentence.

The week's sell-off, according to CNBC, was driven by investor worries about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. SK Hynix and Seoul Semiconductor fell alongside U.S. giants such as Nvidia. For context, the U.S. Fed funds rate stands at 3.88%, the 10-year Treasury yields 5.1%, and inflation was 3.74% as of the latest reading, so the rate-hike anxiety is not coming from nowhere.

Lee also addressed the volatility of South Korea's stock market this year. He blamed the chip sector's large weight in the market, noting that semiconductors make up a bigger share of the economy there than in other countries. Translation: when one industry is that large, the national index mostly measures how that industry feels today. Lee still called the broader economy 'solid.'

A less festive view appeared Thursday in the Maeil Business Newspaper, a prominent South Korean publication. According to a CNBC translation, a column urged the government to prepare for an eventual slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. It cited two experts who expect a 'flood of new supply' that would turn the memory market 'into a red ocean' by 2029. A red ocean, in business jargon, is one where many competitors fight over the same customers until the water is the color of margins.

The minister's timeline and the columnist's are not strictly in conflict. Lee said the growth lasts through next year, while the column pointed to 2029. That leaves roughly two years in which everyone is correct and nobody has to plan, which is a comfortable place for a government to be.

The fiscal side is where Lee sounded most content. He said the country expects to collect more tax than initially projected this year and will end up in a stronger fiscal position because of the chip boom. In other words, the stock market gets the nerves and the treasury gets the money.
What to watch: whether the new factory capacity arrives before the demand leaves. Both are possible. Only one of them shows up in the budget.
articles.wire_headline: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
